reviews.review:
Whodunnit needs work. It's not a finished product, and I think the developer made a mistake going for case quantity over quality. There are enough design issues here that I struggled to keep this review from turning into a description of the entire game.

- The main menu's white font over a transparent black background layered on a mixed-color image is genuinely difficult to read. The scenario selection screen looks like it was phoned in, a recurring theme throughout this game. It was not at all clear how to start a case, or even that this was a scenario selection screen. Not a label to be seen anywhere. I had to guess that the left side represents difficulty. Maybe that's part of the mystery. I'm really not sure how this menu got through any kind of playtesting.

- Once you start a case, there's no explanation of what you're supposed to do to solve it or what your tools are. I wouldn't have figured out how to play if the only other review on this game hadn't laid it out in detail (thanks Sosich!)

- The surveillance menu also needs to be redone. It makes no sense that recording and monitoring are separate functions, or that you have to manually select when to record, or that you only get three recording slots. It took me multiple failed runs to figure out that after you select the time and room you want to record in, the thing that looks like a bullet point next to the room dropdown is actually a button that initiates the recording.

- The suspect information sheets are one of the worst parts of this game and an absolute phoned-it-in moment. Instead of creating actual characters for fully developed scenarios, the developer built a bank of character traits that get randomly assigned to suspect files at the start of each case. These traits have nothing to do with the crime. They're just a list of eight throwaway facts like "doesn't know how to boil water." Why you wouldn't write actual suspect profiles in a murder mystery game is beyond me.

- Worse, these random traits are used to gatekeep your two investigation tools: the phone and breaking into people's rooms. So you just have to remember that Edgar can't boil water, or you're locked out of that room or phone call for a period of time. That doesn't add anything to the experience, it just gives you random noise to memorize for no reason.

- The clue system is where you can see the developer's potential. Pointer clues tell you to surveil a specific place at a specific time are fine, functional. The surveillance recordings themselves are probably the only genuinely good writing in the game. On the phone, you can ask suspects several types of questions, like "what do you think of X as the murder weapon" where X could be gun, poison, knife, and so on. The suspect faces reacting to you getting close to the truth is a nice touch and the meta around suspects is clever.

They clearly spent time engineering difficulty into the mysteries and trying not to be obtuse about it. They ruin all of that effort by slapping bad randomized character writing, mechanics that serve no purpose but to exist, and bad UI design on top. The developer should've spent more time on the fundamentals and less time packing the game with scenarios. I was pleasantly surprised to see they're actively developing (there was a patch in June), but it doesn't seem like they've gotten enough critical feedback, or they're ignoring the feedback they do get, because this is really, really bad.
